extracted.intended_audience: regulatory researchers, policy analysts, and agency staff interested in measuring the influence of public comments on rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating how and whether public comments influence regulatory rulemaking outcomes using quantitative, qualitative, testimonial, and automated text-analysis methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantifiable Changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Tracking measurable modifications between proposed and final rules (e.g., 'dollar amounts of government allocations') and correlating these shifts with submitted comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use observable, numeric changes in rule text or regulatory outputs as outcome variables; statistically link those changes to comment content, timing, or submitter characteristics to infer influence. Example given: tracking dollar amounts of allocations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manual Content Coding
rubrics_metrics.description: Hand-analyzing the substance of comments alongside regulatory revisions to identify connections between what commenters argued and how the rule changed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manually code comments for topics, recommendations, and positions, then compare coded themes to edits in the rulemaking record to assess whether and how comment content maps onto regulatory revisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulator Testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: Relying on statements from agency officials describing instances where comments shaped their decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine public statements, guidance documents, preambles, or testimony by regulators that explicitly attribute certain changes or decisions to submitted comments as direct evidence of influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topic Modeling (RegRank)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying automated natural language processing (RegRank) to assess the 'structure and sentiment' of documents and determine alignment between comment tones and final rule adjustments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use algorithmic approaches (topic models, sentiment analysis, network-style rankings like RegRank) to quantify content structure and sentiment across large comment corpora and compare those signals to patterns in final rules to infer directional alignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Directional Alignment of Rule Changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Measuring whether agencies adjusted rules directionally toward the substance of submitted comments — i.e., final rules moved in the direction advocated by commenters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalize 'direction' for relevant policy variables and test if changes from proposed to final rule correlate with the substantive direction of comments; used in the study's conclusion that 'comments mattered' because agencies adjusted rules toward comment substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differential Influence by Commenter Type
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessing whether influence varies across submitter groups (e.g., industry, public interest, individuals), as the study found finance industry comments held substantially greater influence than other occupational groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disaggregate comments by submitter occupation/affiliation and compare estimated influence measures (e.g., effect sizes on rule changes or alignment scores) to detect unequal impacts across groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect on Finalization Likelihood
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluating whether submission of comments affects the probability that a rulemaking proceeds to finalization, noting the finding that public interest comments increased finalization likelihood though they showed less direct influence on rule substance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model the relationship between comment submission patterns (volume, type, timing) and downstream procedural outcomes (e.g., whether and when a rule is finalized), distinguishing procedural influence (likelihood/timing) from substantive change influence.
